reflection_q3: Your concept here is ok but i fear it’s largely a feel good program.   Many things noted sound good but need to be reviewed at a much more real world level.  Fussing about taxing the wealthy more sounds great but you need to recognize that roughly 20% of the top income earning folks already pay roughly 80%of the federal income tax collected.  Jump it up more and these smart affluent folks will make moves to counter these slick moves you suggest.  Look no further than the real world outcomes when New York, Chicago and other s just pump up their tax burden on the affluent and then wonder “where did they go”?  They leave those locations and the great forecast income stream almost always fails to arrive.  CA is also a prime example of this.  My own family business departed CA years ago for just these reasons.   I would much prefer less “Washington DC centric solutions and shove what you can back to the state level.  State representatives are much more accountable to their populations than the clowns we have in DC.

reflection_q3: Thank you for the amazing and hard work to put his together. When I read this I am frequently confused about what is the outcome that you want to achieve in each section. Just telling me the problem and giving me options to choose from does not tell me what it is you want to achieve, or why your proposed solution will get us there. I am not excited when I read this, I am actually skeptical thinking this is just the same old stuff. For instance spending more money for education and for testing will not change the worst education system in the free world. There must be better ways to do this? To get people motivated and excited about the possibility of change and moving forward with solutions that work for everyone (or at least most), the millions and not the few. Thank you, for taking the time to read this.

reflection_q3: I don't want expanded school choice or "more teacher accountability." I want strong public schools that are funded adequately, with teachers paid commensurate to the value of the work they do, and I don't want those schools' funding and success to be tied to their zip codes. School choice just continues to pull the infrastructure of our educational systems apart. Create public schools that get funded at the same level in Beverly Hills as they do in inner-city Chicago. Give poor kids the same investment that rich kids get, and vice versa. Then see how fast America gets behind good public schooling, when they can't hide behind their geographic privilege.

reflection_q3:
End the electoral college for presidential election and replace it with plain popular vote (the idiosyncracies of the electoral college are long and well known: 1. Discrepancy with the popular vote; 2. Voters from small states like Washignton DC and Wyoming have 2.5 times the voting power of voters from, for example, Texas and California; 3. According to polls, it is supported by a minority of US voters). If the process for ending the electoral college is blocked by some vote specified in the constitution, amend the constitution accordingly, why not via a popular vote.
Make Washigton DC a state for the purpose of simplifying formulations such as "... all states and the DC ..." into "... all states ..."

reflection_q3: You're avoiding the most divisive issues, the ones which will attract actual votes to swing district Independent candidates. (1) You must step up and directly support reproductive rights and same sex marriage, even at the risk of alienating the hard right. (2) You must also oppose racial politics which favor criminals and illegal immigrants over police and legal immigration, even if that alienates the rigid left. These "Grand Bargain" issues you frame aren't emotional enough to pull people apart from their loyalties, and the solutions sound like the result of an inoffensive verbal negotiation which might come out of a European parliament. Oh, and by the way, YouGov doesn't claim to use legit survey methodology so citing it will not impress anyone with a research background.

reflection_q3:
Current deficits are unsustainable and will explode due to (1) rising healthcare costs as the population ages, (2) a higher % of the population being retired, and (3) rising interest rates on government debt as investors realize the government cannot pay back its debt.  Raising marginal tax rates won’t help; history shows that marginal rates as high as 94% (under Truman) have not produced more federal revenues as a % of GDP than we’re getting now because the rich stop working and investing (or move abroad).
We have to dramatically reduce healthcare costs.  We can offer plans that cost half as much, as demonstrated by Rosen Hotels & Resorts with their RosenCare model.   Additional savings could be achieved by offering “economy” health plans that (1) provide free unlimited primary care and no co-pays on generic drugs — but require at least annual primary care visits to maximize preventative care, (2) waives the right to sue providers, (3) covers only hospice care once a patient is terminal, (4) only cover the 85% of procedures and drugs that add the most quality adjusted life years per $ invested, (5) tells patients the low-cost provider for whatever they need and only reimburses at their rate.  
Also, premiums should vary based on lifestyle choices, with people who make controllable lifestyle choices (e.g., smoking) paying a premium to cover the expected cost of their poor decision.  Government plans should only offer the economy plan, with patents allowed to “buy-up” to conventional insurance at their own expense.
